| material_system | Si1-xGex and SiGe:C thin epitaxial layers used as HBT base layers (paper mentions nominal SiGe base ~12% Ge in one device flow); SiGeC layers grown by MBE/CVD (general discussion); layers are epitaxial thin films on bonded SOI substrates in HBT process flows. |
| sample_processing_conditions | General conditions discussed: selective epitaxial Si collector grown at 900 °C; non-selective SiGe base and Si emitter cap grown at 750 °C (for the SiGe HBT process described). For SiGeC the paper states low-temperature MBE and CVD are used to obtain SiGeC with substitutional carbon; thermal processing steps discussed include thermal oxidation, implant activation anneals and other post-growth anneals (no numeric anneal times given). The paper emphasises that oxidation generates higher carbon loss rates than vacuum/inert anneals and that Si-cap thickness and overall thermal budget strongly influence C retention and clustering. Growth far from equilibrium (metastable alloys, C supersaturation) is noted but without specific temperature/time data for SiGe:C layers. |
| carbon_concentration_and_form | No quantitative C atomic percent or concentration (cm^-3) values are reported for SiGe:C in this paper. The paper distinguishes total carbon measured by SIMS versus substitutional carbon (Cs) measured/ inferred via HRXRD, Raman and FTIR (FTIR Cs line noted at 610 cm^-1). The paper refers to 'small percentage of substitutional carbon' incorporated during growth (used to suppress B TED), and to C supersaturation in metastable alloys. It also notes the presence of interstitial carbon (Ci) as a consequence of clustering/redistribution during thermal processing. Carbon introduction methods discussed: in-situ doping during epitaxial growth (MBE/CVD) and possible implantation or redistribution during processing (implant damage, oxidation-driven interstitial flux). |
| carbon_residence_site | Discussed sites: substitutional carbon (Cs) on lattice sites (desired), interstitial carbon (Ci) (undesirable), carbon clustering/aggregates and the potential for precipitate formation. Evidence strength: moderate—paper describes which measurement techniques detect total C (SIMS) versus Cs (HRXRD/Raman/FTIR) and indicates disparities between techniques interpreted as differing Cs/Ci ratios; no direct atomic-resolution identification of exact lattice site from this work is presented, but HRTEM is proposed to view clustering. |
| local_environment_preference | Not reported quantitatively. The paper does not provide data or computations on nearest-neighbor preferences (C–Si vs C–Ge bonding) or energies; it only states that substitutional C is used for band engineering and strain control and that 2D growth conditions help obtain substitutional rather than interstitial C. No EXAFS/DFT or coordination statistics are given. |
| carbon_clustering_and_complexes | The paper discusses carbon clustering qualitatively: (i) clustering and redistribution can occur during post-growth thermal processing (oxidation, anneals, implant activation); (ii) clustering can produce Ci and may lead to formation of precipitates (paper text states 'clustering can result in interstitial carbon (Ci) leading to the formation of β-Si precipitates' — quoted as in the manuscript); (iii) methods to detect clustering include HRTEM, HRXRD, FTIR and Raman. No quantitative cluster sizes, densities or structures are reported in this paper. |
| sic_precipitate_presence_and_characterization | The paper does not report confirmed SiC precipitates. It references Si–C vibrational lines (FTIR Si–C lines 700–900 cm^-1) as signatures used to probe Si–C bonding and mentions looking for clustering/precipitates with HRTEM if XRD and SIMS diverge during anneals. The manuscript contains a possibly ambiguous statement about 'β-Si precipitates' following Ci formation; however, no TEM/XRD/Raman evidence for SiC (or specific SiC polytypes) is presented or confirmed in this work. |
| precipitate_morphology_metrics | No quantitative precipitate morphology metrics (size, number density, volume fraction, shape, orientation, interface coherency) are provided in the paper. |
| core_shell_or_composition_gradient | No experimental reports of core–shell precipitates, Si-rich shells, or Ge-depleted shells around precipitates are provided. The paper does not present APT/STEM-EDS compositional profiles around inclusions. |
| thermodynamics_energetics | No numerical thermodynamic or DFT energetics are given. The paper states qualitative thermodynamic points: carbon solubility in Si is low, growth conditions are far from equilibrium (metastable, C supersaturation possible), and substitutional carbon is metastable and can be lost/re-distributed under thermal processing. No formation energies, binding energies, interfacial energies, ΔG values, or computed solubility limits are reported. |
| kinetics_mechanisms | Qualitative kinetic statements only: (i) transient enhanced diffusion (TED) of boron is driven by interstitials and is suppressed by incorporation of substitutional carbon during base growth; (ii) sources of interstitials include implant damage and oxidation; (iii) oxidation produces higher carbon loss rates than vacuum or inert anneals; (iv) C-redistribution or loss, clustering and possible precipitate nucleation can occur during post-growth anneals; (v) the paper emphasises the role of sinks/sources (e.g., Si-cap thickness) and overall thermal budget on C kinetics. No diffusion coefficients, activation energies, nucleation barriers or mathematical growth laws are provided. |
| methods_and_models_used | Experimental and characterisation methods explicitly mentioned: SIMS (total C, B, Ge profiles), high-resolution X-ray diffraction (HRXRD) (Cs inference, layer strain/thickness), Raman spectroscopy, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR: Cs line at 610 cm^-1, Oi at 1100 cm^-1, Si–C lines 700–900 cm^-1), scanning ellipsometry (SE: layer thickness, optical properties, inferred C concentration), high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) for clustering/structural imaging, electrical transistor testing for correlating materials changes with device performance. Device/process modelling tools (Silvaco/ISE) are used elsewhere in paper for electrical simulation but not for atomistic C behavior. No computational atomistic methods (DFT, MD) are reported for carbon energetics in this paper. |
| thermal_conductivity_results | No measurements or computations of lattice or total thermal conductivity, nor any temperature-dependent thermal transport data, are reported for SiGe or SiGe:C in this paper. |
| phonon_scattering_and_transport_mechanisms | The paper does not present any phonon scattering measurements or models linking carbon, clusters, or nanoinclusions to phonon scattering or changes in lattice thermal conductivity. No spectral phonon mean-free-path analysis, BTE/Green-Kubo/Callaway modeling, or TDTR/3-omega data are provided. |
| comparative_controls | Comparisons and contrasts discussed qualitatively: (i) SIMS (total C) versus HRXRD/Raman/FTIR (Cs-sensitive) are compared to derive Cs/Ci inferences; (ii) growth conditions (low-temperature MBE/CVD touted for higher Cs) versus subsequent thermal oxidation/anneals (which can cause C loss and clustering) are compared; (iii) SiGe with and without introduced substitutional C is discussed in context of suppression of B TED (i.e., SiGe vs SiGe:C as process-level comparison). No side-by-side, quantitative material property comparisons (e.g., diffusion rates, energy barriers) are provided in the paper. |
| counterevidence_or_conflicts | The paper explicitly notes that no single technique is sufficient: discrepancies between SIMS and XRD/SE measurements can occur and are interpreted as differences in Cs vs Ci content. The authors state they will seek HRTEM if XRD and SIMS results diverge after annealing. There is no confirmed observation of SiC nanoprecipitates in this work; the paper frames precipitate formation as a possible outcome of clustering under certain thermal conditions, not as a demonstrated result. |
| key_takeaways_claims | (1) Substitutional carbon (Cs) incorporated during epitaxial growth is effective at suppressing transient enhanced diffusion (TED) of boron in SiGe HBT base layers and is therefore desirable for HBT fabrication. (2) Achieving and retaining Cs requires controlled low-temperature epitaxial growth (MBE/CVD) with 2D growth conditions and careful thermal-budget management; oxidation and implant damage increase interstitial fluxes and can cause C loss or clustering. (3) Total carbon (SIMS) versus substitutional carbon (HRXRD/Raman/FTIR) measurements must be correlated to determine Cs/Ci (I/S ratio); HRTEM is used to search for clustering if inconsistencies arise. (4) The paper does not provide quantitative thermodynamic/kinetic parameters, nor any measured impacts of C or potential SiC inclusions on lattice thermal conductivity — those remain outside the data presented here. |

metadata.abstract: We report on a detailed study of the dependence of the vibrational modes in rapid thermal chemical vapor deposited Si1−x−yGexCy films on the substitutional carbon concentration. Si1−x−yGexCy films were investigated using Raman and infrared spectroscopy with x varying in the range of 10%–16% and y in the range of 0%–1.8%. The introduction of C into thin SiGe layers reduces the average lattice constant. It has been shown that the integrated infrared intensity of the Si–C peak and the ratio of both the Raman integrated and peak intensities of the Si–C peak (at ∼605 cm−1) to the Si–Si peak of SiGeC layer, increase linearly with C content and are independent of the Ge content. This leads to the conclusion that infrared absorption and Raman scattering data can be used to determine the fraction of substitutional carbon content in Si1−x−yGexCy layers with a Ge content of up to 16%. It is also shown that the intensity ratio of the carbon satellite peak to the local carbon mode increases linearly with C content up ...

No experimental evidence for interstitial C or Si–C precipitate-phase C within these samples; alternative assignment of the satellite to nonsubstitutional sites is cited from the literature (Rowell et al.) but not supported by the authors' data. |
| local_environment_preference | Reported short-range ordering: increase of the satellite-to-local Si–C intensity ratio with C content is interpreted as an increasing probability of 3nn C–C pairs; authors state (citing theory) that the 3nn configuration is the most strongly bound because short Si–C bonds can be accommodated without strong bond-bending. The paper finds the integrated IR Si–C intensity and the Raman I(C)/I(Si-Si) ratio scale linearly with C content and are independent of Ge content (up to 16%), implying substitutional incorporation is not strongly dependent on Ge fraction in this compositional range. No quantitative binding energies or energetic preference numbers are reported in this paper. |
| carbon_clustering_and_complexes | Evidence for C–C short-range ordering (third-nearest-neighbor pairs): the intensity ratio of the carbon 3nn satellite peak (≈630 cm⁻¹) to the local carbon mode increases linearly with y up to 1.8%, interpreted as increased probability of forming 3nn substitutional C pairs. The authors state carbon pairs (3nn) are preferred; no evidence for larger C clusters, extended aggregates, platelets, or C–vacancy complexes is reported in these samples. |
| sic_precipitate_presence_and_characterization | No SiC precipitates detected: FTIR spectra were inspected in the 750–800 cm⁻¹ region where SiC stretching modes would appear (≈800 cm⁻¹) and no absorption peak was observed for any measured sample; authors explicitly conclude absence of SiC precipitate phase in all samples studied. |
| precipitate_morphology_metrics | None |
| core_shell_or_composition_gradient | None reported. The paper does not present any microscopy/compositional mapping (TEM/EDS/APT) that would identify Si-rich shells or Ge-depleted shells around inclusions; no core–shell features are reported because no precipitates were detected. |
| thermodynamics_energetics | No formation energies, binding energies, interfacial energies, ΔG, solubility limits, or explicit thermodynamic numbers are reported in this work. The paper cites theoretical/previous work (e.g., Rückert and Methfessel) regarding preferred 3nn carbon pairing and bond accommodation but does not present new computed energetics. |
| kinetics_mechanisms | No experimental or computed kinetic parameters (diffusion coefficients, activation energies, nucleation barriers, growth rates, time–temperature–precipitation behavior) are reported. The authors do not present data on C diffusion, nucleation, or growth kinetics of SiC; they only report absence of SiC precipitates in as-grown RTCVD films under the reported growth conditions. |
| methods_and_models_used | Experimental: Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy (normal incidence, micro-sampling, MCT detector), Raman spectroscopy (514 nm Ar+ excitation, backscattering micro-Raman), Rutherford backscattering spectroscopy (RBS) for Ge content, x-ray diffraction (XRD) for substitutional C concentration, spectral peak fitting using Gaussian/Lorentzian components; data analysis: linear fits of integrated intensities and peak-intensity ratios versus substitutional C fraction. The paper references theoretical calculations from the literature but does not perform new DFT/atomistic calculations itself. |
| thermal_conductivity_results | None |
| phonon_scattering_and_transport_mechanisms | Indirect spectroscopic evidence that carbon incorporation strongly perturbs local bonds and phonon frequencies: (i) Si–Si Raman peak shifts to lower frequency with increasing C content (linear dependence reported, slope depends on Ge content), and (ii) both local (~605 cm⁻¹) and satellite Si–C mode frequencies increase with C content; authors attribute shifts to large local bond distortion induced by substitutional C. No measurements or quantitative models of lattice thermal conductivity, phonon mean free paths, or explicit scattering rates are reported, nor are there fits to phonon-transport models (Callaway/BTE) in this paper. |
| comparative_controls | Direct comparisons made between SiGe reference films without carbon and SiGeC films (spectral subtraction used). Multiple sample sets with different Ge (≈9–16%) and C (0–1.8%) contents were compared; the key comparative observations are that Si–C IR and Raman signal scaling with y is independent of Ge content up to 16%, and that the presence/strength of the satellite peak correlates with y. No pre/post anneal or precipitate-containing vs precipitate-free comparisons (other than as-grown carbon-free vs carbon-containing) are presented. |
| counterevidence_or_conflicts | The paper notes conflicting attributions in prior literature: Rowell et al. assigned the ≈630 cm⁻¹ satellite to nonsubstitutional carbon, whereas other works (Guédj et al., Rücker et al., and theoretical studies) attribute it to 3nn substitutional C pairs; this work supports the 3nn interpretation. The authors also note disparate literature reports regarding the direction/magnitude of Si–Si and Si–Ge Raman peak shifts with C content; their measurements show Si–Si peak softening with increasing C for their sample sets. |
| key_takeaways_claims | 1) Substitutional carbon incorporation is confirmed by the presence of a Si–C local vibrational mode at ≈605 cm⁻¹; both FTIR integrated intensity and Raman I(C)/I(Si–Si) scale linearly with substitutional C content (y) and are essentially independent of Ge content up to x≈16%. 2) A Raman satellite near ≈630 cm⁻¹ grows with y and is attributed to third-nearest-neighbor substitutional C–C pairs (short-range ordering), with the satellite/local intensity ratio increasing linearly up to y=1.8%. 3) No SiC precipitates are observed (no ≈800 cm⁻¹ SiC band), implying that under the reported RTCVD growth conditions (≈550 °C, 1 Torr) and C contents ≤1.8 at.% the carbon remains substitutional/short-range ordered rather than forming SiC precipitates. 4) Carbon incorporation produces pronounced local bond distortions that shift phonon frequencies (Si–Si softening; Si–C hardening) but the paper provides no data on thermal conductivity or precipitation kinetics. |
| additional_spectral_relations | Reported linear relations for Si–C Raman peaks vs y: ω_Si-C (satellite) = 623.9 + 229.3 y (cm⁻¹) and ω_Si-C (local) = 604.3 + 229.3 y (cm⁻¹); FTIR integrated Si–C intensity scales linearly with substitutional C, fit A_int ≈ 0.39 y (this work) and previously A_int ≈ 0.34 y (Finkman et al.). Raman intensity ratio I(C)/I(Si–Si) ≈ 0.0303 y (integrated) and peak-intensity relation I(C)/I(Si–Si) ≈ 0.0117 y (peak). |

metadata.title: Si and SiGe Nanowire for Micro-Thermoelectric Generator: A Review of the Current State of the Art
metadata.abstract: In our environment, the large availability of wasted heat has motivated the search for methods to harvest heat. As a reliable way to supply energy, SiGe has been used for thermoelectric generators (TEGs) in space missions for decades. Recently, micro-thermoelectric generators (μTEG) have been shown to be a promising way to supply energy for the Internet of Things (IoT) by using daily waste heat. Combining the predominant CMOS compatibility with high electric conductivity and low thermal conductivity performance, Si nanowire and SiGe nanowire have been a candidate for μTEG. This review gives a comprehensive introduction of the Si, SiGe nanowires, and their possibility for μTEG. The basic thermoelectric principles, materials, structures, fabrication, measurements, and applications are discussed in depth.

| citation_title | Si and SiGe Nanowire for Micro-Thermoelectric Generator: A Review of the Current State of the Art |

| sample_processing_conditions | Reported methods in cited literature: NEMD simulations of β‑SiC and SiC NWs; experimental placement of individual and double β‑SiC NWs on electrodes via focused ion beam manipulation followed by 3ω thermal measurements; temperature ranges for measurement typically 190–370 K in cited experimental works. The review does not give detailed growth temperatures/times for the NWs in these summaries. |
| carbon_concentration_and_form | Not applicable — SiC is a stoichiometric compound (Si and C) in these discussions (i.e., separate SiC nanowire material), not carbon dopant in SiGe. |
| carbon_residence_site | Not applicable for SiC nanowires (C occupies the carbide sublattice of SiC). |
| local_environment_preference | Not applicable (in SiC the C is bonded to Si in the carbide structure); review does not discuss substitutional preference in mixed SiGe matrices because these SiC items are standalone materials. |
| carbon_clustering_and_complexes | Not discussed in the context of SiC nanowires (SiC being a crystalline carbide rather than C clusters in SiGe). |
| sic_precipitate_presence_and_characterization | The review does not report SiC precipitates inside SiGe; it summarizes studies of freestanding SiC nanowires and their characterization (experimental 3ω measurements, NEMD simulations). No mention of SiC polytype for precipitates in SiGe is given. |
| precipitate_morphology_metrics | For SiC NW material (cited): simulations and experiments consider NW diameters down to ~4 nm (simulation result cited); experimental 3ω measurements reported thermal conductivities for individual and double β‑SiC NWs but the review does not give a full statistical size distribution or number density for precipitates because these are freestanding NW samples, not precipitates in an alloy matrix. |
| core_shell_or_composition_gradient | No reports in the review of Si-rich shells or Ge-depleted shells around SiC inclusions in SiGe (SiC discussed only as separate NW material). |
| thermodynamics_energetics | The review summarizes thermal-transport results but does not provide formation energies, interfacial energies, or phase stability data for SiC precipitation in SiGe. |
| kinetics_mechanisms | No diffusion coefficients, nucleation barriers, or kinetic growth laws for SiC precipitates in SiGe are given; the review only reports that NW thermal conductivity depends strongly on diameter and length (size confinement and boundary scattering effects). |
| methods_and_models_used | Methods cited in the review for SiC studies include non-equilibrium molecular dynamics (NEMD) simulations, equilibrium MD, focused-ion-beam manipulation of NWs, and experimental 3ω thermal-conductivity measurements; TEM and transport (Seebeck) measurements were also referenced in the cited experimental studies. |
| thermal_conductivity_results | Numbers cited in the review: NEMD simulations predicted lattice thermal conductivity of SiC NWs in the range ~4–12 W·m^-1·K^-1 with a value near ~5 W·m^-1·K^-1 for ≈4 nm diameter NWs (Termentzidis et al., 2013 cited). Experimental 3ω measurements reported thermal conductivities of individual and double β‑SiC NWs as 82 ± 6 and 73 ± 5 W·m^-1·K^-1 (Lee et al., 2010 cited) — note the large difference between simulation for very small diameters and experiment for (larger) measured NWs. Seebeck coefficients for N‑type SiC NWs at 300 K reported between −22 and −56 μV·K^-1 (Valentin et al., 2013 as cited). |
| phonon_scattering_and_transport_mechanisms | The review attributes reduced thermal conductivity in SiC NWs to phonon boundary scattering and size (confinement) effects; MD/NEMD studies indicate diameter and length strongly affect κ, consistent with phonon mean‑free‑path truncation and enhanced boundary scattering in nanoscale wires. |
| comparative_controls | Comparisons summarized: bulk β‑SiC vs SiC nanowires (nanowires show dramatically reduced κ); NWs with varying diameters and lengths (κ increases with both diameter and length). Different polytypes and diameter modulation were simulated with similar trends. |
| counterevidence_or_conflicts | The review highlights variation in reported κ between simulations and experiments (e.g., very low simulated κ for ≈4 nm vs much higher experimental κ for larger measured NWs), reflecting sensitivity to diameter, polytype, measurement technique, and sample quality. |
| key_takeaways_claims | (i) SiC as a separate Group‑IV carbide shows strong size-dependent reduction of lattice thermal conductivity in nanowire form; (ii) MD/NEMD simulations predict very low κ for sub‑10 nm SiC NWs, while experiments on larger NWs report much higher κ, indicating strong dimensional and sample-dependence; (iii) the review contains no direct observations or characterization of SiC nanoinclusions/precipitates inside Si1−xGex, nor any reported quantitative impact of SiC precipitates or C incorporation on SiGe lattice thermal conductivity or phonon scattering. |

metadata.title: Gas Source Techniques for Molecular Beam Epitaxy of Highly Mismatched Ge Alloys
metadata.abstract: Ge and its alloys are attractive candidates for a laser compatible with silicon integrated circuits. Dilute germanium carbide (Ge1−xCx) offers a particularly interesting prospect. By using a precursor gas with a Ge4C core, C can be preferentially incorporated in substitutional sites, suppressing interstitial and C cluster defects. We present a method of reproducible and upscalable gas synthesis of tetrakis(germyl)methane, or (H3Ge)4C, followed by the design of a hybrid gas/solid-source molecular beam epitaxy system and subsequent growth of defect-free Ge1−xCx by molecular beam epitaxy (MBE). Secondary ion mass spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy and contactless electroreflectance confirm the presence of carbon with very high crystal quality resulting in a decrease in the direct bandgap energy. This technique has broad applicability to growth of highly mismatched alloys by MBE.

| citation_title | here |
| mention_or_use | use |
| material_system | Ge1-xCx dilute germanium-carbide heterostructures grown as 20 nm Ge1-xCx wells with 50 nm Ge barriers on GaAs(100) (GaAs buffer + 50 nm AlAs back barrier); reported C atomic fractions: SIMS plateaus ~0.03% and ~0.05% averaged over superlattice, equivalent to ~0.2% C in Ge1-xCx wells (for wells/barriers described). |
| sample_processing_conditions | Hybrid gas-source/solid-source MBE on GaAs(100) with initial 10 nm solid-source Ge at 400 °C (thermocouple), growth cycles with (H3Ge)4C gas injected (foreline pressure 30 mTorr for 20 s, chamber pressure rose to 5×10^-5 Torr), repeated cycles producing 20 nm Ge1-xCx wells and 50 nm Ge barriers; substrate temperatures studied up to 525 °C; incorporation increases at T_sub ≥ 450 °C, growth roughening/Ge–C bond breakage observed above ≈475 °C. LN2 cryoshroud turned off for gas growth; ion pump off during growth to maximize incorporation. |
| carbon_concentration_and_form | Reported average SIMS plateaus ≈0.03% and ≈0.05% C (averaged over rough superlattice); authors estimate this corresponds to ≈0.2 at.% C in the 20 nm Ge1-xCx wells for runs with T_sub ≥ 450 °C. Carbon was introduced in situ via the molecular precursor (H3Ge)4C (4GeMe). Chemical form in the lattice is reported as substitutional/sp3-like C incorporated as part of the Ge4C-derived local motif (no evidence of graphitic C clusters detected by HRTEM, Raman, NRA-RBS, STEM-EDX). |
| carbon_residence_site | Authors conclude C is incorporation-substitutional (sp3) in the Ge diamond lattice (i.e., on Ge lattice sites or in Ge4C local building block), motivated by: (i) precursor design (C fully surrounded by Ge in 4GeMe), (ii) absence of C-clusters by TEM/Raman/NRA-RBS/STEM-EDX, and (iii) bandgap reduction consistent with dilute substitutional C. Paper explicitly notes that in the precursor C atoms are third-nearest neighbors at minimum (designed spacing). Strength of evidence: experimental (structural null detection of clusters) + spectroscopic (CER band shift); no direct atomic-site-resolved measurement (e.g., APT or EXAFS) presented in this paper. |
| local_environment_preference | Paper does not present measurements directly comparing C–Si vs C–Ge bonding preferences; the work focuses on C incorporation into Ge where C is delivered already bonded to Ge in the 4GeMe precursor. C–Ge bond elongation value from cited literature: Ge–C bond length elongated ≈5% to ≈2.05 Å (reported in background) for E4C-type compounds; Si–C elongation cited as ≈7% (1.89 Å) for E=Si in prior literature. No quantitative DFT energetics comparing C–Si vs C–Ge provided in this paper (references to prior ab initio work are cited). |
| carbon_clustering_and_complexes | Historical context: prior growth attempts produced graphitic clusters and numerous C–C point defects (literature cited). In this work: multiple characterization methods (HRTEM/STEM-EDX/Raman/NRA-RBS) report no detectable C–C clusters or graphitic inclusions in the grown Ge1-xCx layers at the reported low concentrations. Authors attribute absence of clustering to the use of a Ge4C-core precursor which sterically/chemically prevents exposed bare C on the growth surface. No direct identification of point complexes (e.g., C–vacancy complexes, split interstitials) is reported. |
| sic_precipitate_presence_and_characterization | No SiC precipitates or SiC-related phases are reported or observed. The paper contains no TEM/EDS/EELS/XRD/Raman evidence for SiC inclusions in these Ge-based samples; SiC precipitation is not discussed as an observed phenomenon in the experiments. |
| precipitate_morphology_metrics | Not applicable / not reported (no precipitates or nanoinclusions of SiC observed in this work). |
| core_shell_or_composition_gradient | No reports of Si-rich shells, Ge-depleted shells, or composition gradients around SiC inclusions (no inclusions observed). SIMS profiles show plateaus of C averaged over rough superlattice; authors note SIMS spatial averaging and limited resolution causing smearing due to surface roughness. No APT/STEM-EELS linescans showing local gradients presented. |
| thermodynamics_energetics | Paper provides limited thermodynamic/energetic data: (i) literature bulk solubility cited: C in Ge may be as low as 10^8 cm^-3 (citation 13). (ii) Bond dissociation energies used to motivate precursor chemistry: Ge–C ≈ 255 kJ/mol; Ge–H ≈ 290 kJ/mol; Ge–Cl ≈ 356 kJ/mol; Ge–Br ≈ 276 kJ/mol; Ge–Ge ≈ 256 kJ/mol (values cited/discussed in context of precursor stability and cracking). (iii) Critical-thickness estimates (strain/thermodynamic stability context): People–Bean model predicts critical thickness ≈1250 nm for 1% C Ge1-xCx on Ge; Matthews–Blakeslee model predicts ≈36 nm for the same composition (cited models). No first-principles formation energies, binding energies for substitutional vs interstitial C, interface energies, or ΔG of SiC precipitation are presented in this paper (such calculations are referenced in prior work but not given here). |
| kinetics_mechanisms | Qualitative kinetic information: MBE is kinetically limited enabling incorporation beyond equilibrium solubility; incorporation efficiency depends on growth/substrate temperature and precursor cracking/sticking: authors report incomplete incorporation below ≈450 °C and improved incorporation at ≥450 °C; above ≈475 °C surface roughening is observed and is attributed to Ge–C bond breakage and altered kinetics. Authors note a change in growth kinetics above ≈475 °C attributed to chemisorption of (H3Ge)4C and H2-passivation of the surface. No quantitative diffusion coefficients, activation energies for C diffusion/nucleation, nucleation barriers, or growth-rate laws for precipitation are provided. |
| methods_and_models_used | Experimental methods: hybrid gas-source/solid-source molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) with (H3Ge)4C precursor, SIMS (Evans Analytical Group), TEM/HRTEM/STEM-EDX, Raman spectroscopy, NRA-RBS, contactless electroreflectance (CER), gas-phase FT-IR, 1D/2D NMR and ESMS for precursor characterization. Models/theory invoked: band anticrossing concept and prior hybrid DFT predictions (ref. 7) for band structure of dilute GeC; People–Bean and Matthews–Blakeslee critical-thickness models for strain stability; ionization cross-section/sensitivity-factor arguments for SIMS quantification; simple molecular-flow conductance estimate for gas delivery line. |
| thermal_conductivity_results | No measurements or computations of lattice or total thermal conductivity or thermal transport in Ge1-xCx/SiGe:C are reported in this paper. |
| phonon_scattering_and_transport_mechanisms | No experimental or modeled analysis of phonon scattering, mean-free-path spectra, or thermal resistance associated with substitutional C or hypothetical SiC nanoinclusions is presented in this work. |
| comparative_controls | Comparisons made in the paper include: (i) pure Ge direct bandgap (0.80 eV) vs Ge:C sample direct bandgap (0.776 eV) from CER showing 24 meV reduction; (ii) growth temperature dependence: lower T shows incomplete incorporation, ≥450 °C yields higher incorporation, >475 °C causes roughening; (iii) prior literature reports where C clustering/graphitic defects were observed vs the current results showing no detectable clusters when using 4GeMe. |
| counterevidence_or_conflicts | Paper highlights that prior growth methods often produced graphitic C clusters and midgap traps, whereas their MBE with 4GeMe shows no detectable clusters at reported low C contents. They also caution that SIMS spatial averaging and sample roughness smear profiles, so SIMS values are averaged and may not represent local well concentrations precisely. No direct site-specific atom-probe or EXAFS evidence is provided to irrefutably prove substitutional C at the atomic scale; the interpretation rests on indirect evidence (absence of clusters + bandgap shift). |
| key_takeaways_claims | 1) Using a Ge4C-core precursor (H3Ge)4C enables incorporation of carbon into Ge as substitutional/sp3-like species without detectable graphitic C clusters at dilute concentrations (~0.2 at.% in wells estimated). 2) Incorporation efficiency requires a temperature window: ≈450 °C for effective incorporation while remaining below ≈475 °C to avoid Ge–C bond dissociation and surface roughening. 3) Even very dilute incorporated C produces a measurable 24 meV reduction in the Ge direct bandgap (CER), consistent with theoretical band-anticrossing predictions for dilute GeC. 4) No SiC precipitation, Si-rich shells, or nanoinclusions are observed in these samples at the reported conditions/concentrations. |

| precipitate_morphology_metrics | Not reported in this paper for SiGe:C; readers are referred to cited literature for detailed observations. |
| core_shell_or_composition_gradient | Not reported here; the paper only broadly references prior literature on ordered structures and heteroatomic tetrals that may influence local bonding. |
| thermodynamics_energetics | The paper cites the very low thermodynamic bulk solubility of mismatched elements (e.g., C in Ge potentially as low as 10^8 cm^-3 from Scace & Slack) to motivate kinetically-limited MBE growth; no new thermodynamic formation energies or interfacial energetics for SiGe:C/SiC are provided in this work (the paper references prior ab initio studies on C incorporation). |

paper-ed370b81064857475585dade7616970e8d.displayLabel: Gas Source Techniques for Molecular Beam Epitaxy of Highly Mismatched Ge Alloys

s2Metadata.title: Gas Source Techniques for Molecular Beam Epitaxy of Highly Mismatched Ge Alloys
s2Metadata.abstract: Ge and its alloys are attractive candidates for a laser compatible with silicon integrated circuits. Dilute germanium carbide (Ge1−xCx) offers a particularly interesting prospect. By using a precursor gas with a Ge4C core, C can be preferentially incorporated in substitutional sites, suppressing interstitial and C cluster defects. We present a method of reproducible and upscalable gas synthesis of tetrakis(germyl)methane, or (H3Ge)4C, followed by the design of a hybrid gas/solid-source molecular beam epitaxy system and subsequent growth of defect-free Ge1−xCx by molecular beam epitaxy (MBE). Secondary ion mass spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy and contactless electroreflectance confirm the presence of carbon with very high crystal quality resulting in a decrease in the direct bandgap energy. This technique has broad applicability to growth of highly mismatched alloys by MBE.

content.title: Kinetic trapping yields predominantly substitutional C and suppresses detectable SiC in as-grown films

content.text: If growth is sufficiently kinetically constrained, carbon stays on lattice sites (substitutional) and doesn’t show SiC precipitates in as-grown material, within the experiments’ detection limits.
**Supporting evidence:**

- RTCVD Si1-x-yGexCy: a Si–C local vibrational mode near ~605 cm−1 is stated to originate only from substitutional carbon; linear scaling of IR/Raman C signals with y is consistent with predominant Cs incorporation up to y=1.8%.  <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper>

- RTCVD Si1-x-yGexCy: FTIR inspection in the 750–800 cm−1 region finds no absorption peak near ~800 cm−1; authors explicitly conclude absence of SiC precipitate phase in all studied as-grown samples.  <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper>

- Ge1-xCx MBE with (H3Ge)4C precursor: multiple structural/spectroscopic probes (TEM/HRTEM/Raman/NRA-RBS/STEM-EDX) report no detectable C–C clusters/graphitic inclusions at dilute C; authors interpret incorporation as substitutional/sp3-like and observe a 24 meV direct-gap reduction consistent with dilute substitutional C effects.  <paper entityId="paper-ed370b81064857475585dade7616970e8d40c981" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="14320628" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Stephenson et al., 2016</paper>

- Process-focused SiGe:C discussion: emphasizes growth far from equilibrium (metastable alloys, C supersaturation possible) and that substitutional carbon is desired/obtained under appropriate growth conditions but can be lost/redistributed under subsequent thermal processing.  <paper entityId="paper-f253d7c4609a7c200caeda07a88dc222ba55cad2" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="137240377" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Hall et al., 2004</paper>

content.title: Substitutional carbon exhibits increasing 3nn C–C short-range order with increasing Cs fraction

content.text: As substitutional carbon increases (up to ~1.8%), more of it forms preferred, spaced substitutional pairs (3rd-nearest neighbors) rather than precipitating as SiC in the as-grown state.
**Supporting evidence:**

- RTCVD Si1-x-yGexCy: a Raman satellite near ~630 cm−1 is reported; its intensity relative to the local Si–C mode increases linearly with y and is attributed to 3nn substitutional C–C pairs; authors cite theory that 3nn is most strongly bound because short Si–C bonds can be accommodated without strong bond-bending.  <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper>

- RTCVD Si1-x-yGexCy: despite increasing y to 1.8%, FTIR shows no SiC precipitate band near ~800 cm−1, supporting that increasing carbon first manifests as substitutional ordering rather than detectable SiC precipitation in as-grown samples.  <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper>

content.title: Defect-injecting thermal processing increases carbon redistribution/clustering propensity relative to inert anneals

content.text: Processing that generates many defects (oxidation, implantation) makes carbon move and cluster more than inert annealing does, enabling precipitation routes.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Process discussion reports that oxidation produces higher carbon loss rates than vacuum/inert anneals and that carbon redistribution/clustering can occur during thermal processing; clustering can produce interstitial carbon (Ci) as an outcome of redistribution under processing steps (qualitative).  <paper entityId="paper-f253d7c4609a7c200caeda07a88dc222ba55cad2" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="137240377" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Hall et al., 2004</paper>

content.title: SiC-like precipitation requires (and promotes) Si-rich local environments; Ge-depleted shells are a plausible but not yet evidenced consequence

content.text: Mobile carbon is expected to form SiC-like environments when it precipitates, so precipitation should favor Si-rich regions and may push Ge away locally—though that shell effect isn’t directly shown in the provided evidence.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Provided evidence establishes that under certain as-grown RTCVD conditions, SiC precipitates are not observed up to y=1.8% Cs, implying precipitation is not inevitable and requires access to additional pathways (mobility/kinetics), consistent with the need for a mobility-enabling step before precipitation.  <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper>

- Process discussion emphasizes carbon metastability/supersaturation and that thermal processing can cause clustering/redistribution and possible precipitate formation (not directly observed here), consistent with a thermodynamic driving force that is only realized when kinetics allow.  <paper entityId="paper-f253d7c4609a7c200caeda07a88dc222ba55cad2" annotationId="ann_009" corpusId="137240377" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Hall et al., 2004</paper>

- This statement was inferred abductively from: (i) the strong empirical emphasis on substitutional Si–C bonding signatures in SiGeC without SiC precipitates in as-grown films (e5.0), (ii) the general materials-chemistry fact that SiC is a robust stable compound in the Si–C system whereas diamond-structured GeC is far less commonly stable under typical semiconductor processing conditions, and (iii) the mission context (external to the listed evidence) that modeling assumes carbon prefers Si neighbors and explores Si-rich shells around SiC inclusions. The provided sources themselves do not quantify C–Si vs C–Ge preference or report shells.

- If RTCVD Si1-x-yGexCy films (e.g., x≈0.1–0.2, y≈0.5–1.5%) are subjected to an oxidation step versus an inert anneal at comparable peak temperature, then Cs proxies (e.g., 605 cm−1 Si–C local-mode strength per unit total C) will decrease more in the oxidized samples, and SIMS(total C) vs XRD-inferred Cs will diverge more strongly after oxidation than after inert anneal.
- For as-grown RTCVD Si1-x-yGexCy up to y=1.8%, FTIR will continue to show no ~800 cm−1 SiC band while the Raman ~630 cm−1 satellite/local ratio increases approximately linearly with y (within the same growth window).
- In Ge1-xCx grown with the Ge4C-core precursor, raising substrate temperature beyond the reported roughening/bond-breakage threshold (>~475 °C) will increase the likelihood of carbon clustering signatures (Raman/TEM), consistent with loss of kinetic control.

- If a SiGe:C sample is annealed under conditions that intentionally inject interstitials (e.g., oxidation or engineered interstitial injection without oxidation), then APT or STEM-EELS/EDS will reveal nanoscale carbon-rich regions; whether these become crystalline SiC and whether they display a Ge-depleted shell will depend sensitively on x (Ge fraction) and defect flux—this could validate or refute the proposed shell corollary.
- A controlled experiment holding total C fixed but patterning local Si/Ge ratio (e.g., compositional modulation) will show that precipitation onset correlates more strongly with local Si availability than with global x, implying a local-neighborhood-controlled nucleation barrier rather than a purely bulk-composition criterion.
- Rapid quench from melt/near-melt conditions (additive-manufacturing-like) could trap non-crystalline ‘carbidic’ clusters whose vibrational signatures fall between substitutional Si–C modes and crystalline SiC; confirming such intermediates would expand the pathway set beyond Cs/Ci/SiC.

- If oxidation steps do not measurably increase Cs loss/redistribution relative to inert anneals (no change in SIMS-vs-XRD/FTIR/Raman Cs proxies), then the ‘defect-injection switch’ mechanism would be undermined.
- If annealed SiGe:C samples with confirmed SiC precipitates show no preference for Si-rich neighborhoods (e.g., precipitates occur equally in Si-poor regions) and no systematic Ge depletion near inclusions, then the ‘Si-seeking precipitation + shell corollary’ would be weakened.
- If as-grown RTCVD samples at y≤1.8% show a clear ~800 cm−1 SiC FTIR band under the same nominal growth window, then the kinetic-trapping boundary conditions in this theory are incorrect or incomplete.

- No quantitative eV-scale energetics are provided in the evidence for (i) C preference for Si vs Ge nearest neighbors or (ii) the free-energy difference between substitutional C in SiGe and C in a SiC precipitate; thus this theory cannot supply the requested numerical preference magnitudes from the provided sources.  <paper entityId="paper-f253d7c4609a7c200caeda07a88dc222ba55cad2" annotationId="ann_010" corpusId="137240377" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Hall et al., 2004</paper> <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_011" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper> <paper entityId="paper-ed370b81064857475585dade7616970e8d40c981" annotationId="ann_012" corpusId="14320628" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Stephenson et al., 2016</paper>

s2Metadata.title: Si and SiGe Nanowire for Micro-Thermoelectric Generator: A Review of the Current State of the Art
s2Metadata.abstract: In our environment, the large availability of wasted heat has motivated the search for methods to harvest heat. As a reliable way to supply energy, SiGe has been used for thermoelectric generators (TEGs) in space missions for decades. Recently, micro-thermoelectric generators (μTEG) have been shown to be a promising way to supply energy for the Internet of Things (IoT) by using daily waste heat. Combining the predominant CMOS compatibility with high electric conductivity and low thermal conductivity performance, Si nanowire and SiGe nanowire have been a candidate for μTEG. This review gives a comprehensive introduction of the Si, SiGe nanowires, and their possibility for μTEG. The basic thermoelectric principles, materials, structures, fabrication, measurements, and applications are discussed in depth.

s2Metadata.title: Innovative Developpement of Silicon Germanium Alloy Enhanced with Nanoprecipitates by Additive Manufacturing
s2Metadata.abstract: Thermoelectric (TE) devices is presented as an environmentally-friendly technology useful for several niche applications in electricity generation and cooling systems. Recent advances in additive manufacturing (AM) techniques, such as Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), allow manufacturing of a wide range of materials, including TE materials. AM of TE materials open new possibilities in TE devices’ shapes that can facilitate their integration and improve their performance. This work presents the development of silicon germanium (SiGe) alloys by L-PBF process. The first attempt at producing this material resulted in a dense material with promising Seebeck coefficient and thermal conductivity, but its other properties were hindered by mechanical cracking occurring during L-PBF processing. To address this issue, a new approach was studied: nanoprecipitates formation during cooling. Nanoprecipitates can simultaneously enhance TE properties by scattering phonons, and enhance mechanical properties by acting as nucleating agents for silicon germanium matrix, and reduce grain size. It is the first time that such approach is studied in AM of TE materials. A specific study has been performed to define the best nanoprecipitates candidates. Three systems of nanoprecipitates were retained: SiC, WSi2 and MoSi2. This work will present how these nanoprecipitates were chosen, then their impacts on SiGe structural and TE properties.

content.title: Nanoinclusion boundary scattering dominates kappa reduction when inclusion radius is comparable to dominant phonon mean free paths

content.text: At a few nanometers, SiC particle interfaces scatter heat-carrying phonons so much that thermal conductivity can drop more than simple mass/density arguments predict.
**Supporting evidence:**

- SiC nanowire review: MD/NEMD and experiments show strong size dependence of SiC nanowire thermal conductivity, attributed to boundary scattering and mean-free-path truncation, supporting the general principle that nanoscale boundaries strongly reduce lattice kappa.  <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.1">Li et al., 2021</paper>

- Additive manufacturing study motivation: proposes nanoprecipitates (including SiC) to scatter phonons and lower lattice thermal conductivity in SiGe, consistent with boundary/interface scattering as a dominant lever (qualitative).  <paper entityId="paper-ae5f20f78dabfd94851c4851eb2cac2596054626" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="273902266" artifactId="extraction-result-3#uuid-e3.0">Baudry et al., 2024</paper>

content.title: Si-rich / Ge-depleted shells can partially counteract inclusion scattering by reducing alloy disorder and grading impedance

content.text: A Si-rich shell can make the matrix around a particle conduct better by removing Ge disorder, but it also changes interface scattering, so the net effect can go either way and depends on shell thickness.
**Supporting evidence:**

- No direct shell evidence is present in the provided experimental papers; this law is inferred from general alloy-disorder scattering principles plus the mission context that carbon prefers Si neighbors and control runs place particles in Ge-free Si-rich shells.

- RTCVD SiGeC: carbon incorporation perturbs local bonds and phonon frequencies (Si–Si softening; Si–C hardening), indicating that local chemistry can substantially modify vibrational properties, consistent with shells potentially altering local phonon scattering/impedance.  <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper>

- For SiGe at 300 K with SiC inclusions of R~2 nm at low volume fraction, atomistic MD will show a kappa reduction substantially larger than a density-contrast-only bound and closer to a stiffness-contrast-including bound, because elastic mismatch and interface disorder dominate scattering at nm scales.
- Adding a Ge-free Si shell around SiC inclusions will change kappa relative to bare SiGe in a way that depends on shell thickness; thin shells may further reduce kappa (added scattering volume), while intermediate shells may partially recover kappa (reduced alloy disorder near the interface).

- Spectral decomposition (e.g., frequency-resolved heat flux in MD) will show that mid-frequency phonons are most strongly suppressed by SiC inclusions, while low-frequency long-MFP modes are partially transmitted if the shell provides impedance grading; verifying this would enable predictive shell engineering.
- At fixed inclusion size and volume fraction, varying inclusion crystallographic coherency/roughness (coherent vs incoherent interface) will change whether kappa aligns closer to stiffness-contrast or density-contrast bounds; the sign and magnitude could be large.

- If MD shows R~2 nm inclusions reduce kappa only at or below the density-contrast-only bound even with stiff inclusions, then the claim that stiffness mismatch dominates at this scale is incorrect.
- If adding a Ge-free Si shell always decreases (or always increases) kappa monotonically with thickness across a wide range, then the predicted competing-mechanism/non-monotonic behavior is wrong.

- The provided evidence set contains no direct thermal conductivity measurements or simulations for SiGe containing SiC precipitates or shells; thus this theory cannot be directly validated against included data and is built from general principles plus qualitative motivation sources.  <paper entityId="paper-ae5f20f78dabfd94851c4851eb2cac2596054626" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="273902266" artifactId="extraction-result-3#uuid-e3.0">Baudry et al., 2024</paper> <paper entityId="paper-f253d7c4609a7c200caeda07a88dc222ba55cad2" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="137240377" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Hall et al., 2004</paper> <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper> <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.1">Li et al., 2021</paper>

content.title: Three-term competition: inclusion scattering + interface resistance − alloy-disorder relief

content.text: A SiC particle lowers κ by scattering phonons and adding interface resistance, but a Si-rich shell can locally reduce alloy disorder and raise κ; the observed κ is set by the balance.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Proposed strategy in L-PBF SiGe is to form nanoprecipitates (including SiC) specifically to scatter phonons and reduce lattice thermal conductivity, implying inclusion-scattering as a primary mechanism.  <paper entityId="paper-ae5f20f78dabfd94851c4851eb2cac2596054626" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="273902266" artifactId="extraction-result-3#uuid-e3.0">Baudry et al., 2024</paper>

- Review of SiC nanowires emphasizes strong size dependence of κ due to boundary/interface scattering, supporting the importance of nm-scale interfaces for phonon transport.  <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.1">Li et al., 2021</paper>

- RTCVD SiGeC films show substitutional carbon causes strong local bond distortions and phonon-frequency shifts (Si–Si softening; Si–C mode hardening), consistent with strong local vibrational perturbations that can affect scattering and interface mismatch when C/SiC-related features are present.  <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper>

- This statement was logically inferred (abduction) from: (i) the mission statement’s continuum bracketing using density-contrast-only vs stiffness-contrast-only models for SiC spheres (implying at least two inclusion-scattering channels) and (ii) the mission statement’s explicit scenario of a Ge-free (Si-rich) shell around the particle (implying a third, composition-driven modification of intrinsic alloy scattering not included in bare-particle continuum bounds).

content.title: Shell-thickness crossover between (beneficial) disorder relief and (harmful) added scattering area/interfaces

content.text: A very thin Si-rich layer can sometimes slightly help heat flow compared with a bare particle, but a thicker layer usually hurts because it makes the ‘obstacle’ bigger and adds another interface.
**Supporting evidence:**
- Mission context specifies a Ge-free (Si-rich) shell of ~7 Å around the particle in control runs, implying shell thickness is physically relevant and comparable to a few atomic spacings.

- SiC nanowire literature emphasizes that nm-scale boundary scattering can strongly suppress κ, consistent with the idea that adding an additional interface or increasing effective obstacle size can reduce κ.  <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.1">Li et al., 2021</paper>

- This statement was logically inferred (abduction) by combining: (i) the general size dependence of boundary/interface scattering at nanoscales (supported by e6.1) with (ii) the mission’s explicit existence of a finite-thickness, compositionally distinct shell (7 Å), which simultaneously reduces alloy disorder locally and introduces extra scattering geometry.

- At fixed SiC core radius R, κ_lat versus shell thickness t will often be non-monotonic: for very thin, high-quality shells κ_lat can be slightly higher than in the bare-core case (disorder relief dominates), while for thicker shells κ_lat decreases (extra interface/cross-section dominates).
- Increasing the host Ge fraction x (stronger intrinsic alloy scattering) increases the potential κ benefit of a Ge-depleted shell, shifting t* to larger values (thicker shells needed before added scattering dominates).
- Replacing an abrupt Ge-free shell with a graded (Si-rich→matrix) shell of the same outer radius increases κ_lat relative to the abrupt shell because the graded region reduces effective Kapitza resistance (better impedance matching).

- For R≈2 nm, an optimally graded shell could produce an MD κ reduction smaller than what a density-contrast-only continuum lower bound would predict for a bare particle (i.e., the shell acts as an impedance-matching layer for a significant part of the phonon spectrum).
- At sufficient inclusion density, overlapping Ge-depleted shells could create a percolating Si-rich network that increases κ_lat relative to a random homogeneous Si0.8Ge0.2 matrix even while inclusions remain present, yielding a non-intuitive κ versus inclusion density curve (initial decrease then partial recovery).

- If atomistic simulations sweeping shell thickness always show monotonic κ_lat decrease with t (for realistic interface structures), the proposed disorder-relief vs added-scattering crossover mechanism is falsified.
- If an atom-probe or STEM-EDS measurement (in an experimental analog system) finds no meaningful Ge depletion around SiC/C-rich inclusions, then the disorder-relief term is negligible and the theory’s shell mechanism is unsupported.
- If spectral phonon transmission calculations show that graded shells do not reduce interfacial resistance compared with abrupt shells, then the impedance-matching assumption is wrong.

- No provided evidence directly measures κ of SiGe with SiC nanoprecipitates or with Si-rich/Ge-depleted shells; the theory extrapolates from general nanostructure/interface concepts and the mission scenario.  <paper entityId="paper-ae5f20f78dabfd94851c4851eb2cac2596054626" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="273902266" artifactId="extraction-result-3#uuid-e3.0">Baudry et al., 2024</paper> <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.1">Li et al., 2021</paper> <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper>

paper-ed370b81064857475585dade7616970e8d.displayLabel: Gas Source Techniques for Molecular Beam Epitaxy of Highly Mismatched Ge Alloys

s2Metadata.title: Gas Source Techniques for Molecular Beam Epitaxy of Highly Mismatched Ge Alloys
s2Metadata.abstract: Ge and its alloys are attractive candidates for a laser compatible with silicon integrated circuits. Dilute germanium carbide (Ge1−xCx) offers a particularly interesting prospect. By using a precursor gas with a Ge4C core, C can be preferentially incorporated in substitutional sites, suppressing interstitial and C cluster defects. We present a method of reproducible and upscalable gas synthesis of tetrakis(germyl)methane, or (H3Ge)4C, followed by the design of a hybrid gas/solid-source molecular beam epitaxy system and subsequent growth of defect-free Ge1−xCx by molecular beam epitaxy (MBE). Secondary ion mass spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy and contactless electroreflectance confirm the presence of carbon with very high crystal quality resulting in a decrease in the direct bandgap energy. This technique has broad applicability to growth of highly mismatched alloys by MBE.

content.title: Growth-window substitutionality law (Cs dominates; SiC absent in as-grown RTCVD SiGeC up to ~1.8 at.% C)

content.text: Under certain RTCVD growth conditions, carbon stays mostly substitutional and does not form SiC precipitates even up to about 1.8% C.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Si–C local vibrational mode near ~605 cm−1 attributed exclusively to substitutional carbon; integrated FTIR and Raman intensity scale linearly with substitutional carbon y and are essentially independent of Ge content up to 16%.  <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper>

- No SiC precipitates detected: FTIR shows no absorption peak in 750–800 cm−1 region where SiC stretching modes would appear (~800 cm−1); authors conclude absence of SiC precipitate phase in all samples studied.  <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper>

content.title: Thermal-budget/defect-injection law: oxidation/anneals drive Cs→Ci/clustering and possible precipitation

content.text: Heat treatments—especially oxidation and implant-related damage—tend to knock carbon out of substitutional sites, making it mobile and more likely to cluster or precipitate.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Paper discussing SiGe:C in HBT processing emphasizes that substitutional carbon is desired but can be lost/redistributed or cluster during post-growth thermal processing; oxidation generates higher carbon loss rates than vacuum/inert anneals; Si-cap thickness and thermal budget strongly influence retention and clustering.  <paper entityId="paper-f253d7c4609a7c200caeda07a88dc222ba55cad2" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="137240377" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Hall et al., 2004</paper>

- Ge:C MBE study shows incorporation is kinetically limited and temperature-windowed: improved incorporation above ~450 °C but roughening/bond breakage above ~475 °C, illustrating that carbon incorporation state can change when bond stability/kinetics change with temperature.  <paper entityId="paper-ed370b81064857475585dade7616970e8d40c981" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="14320628" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Stephenson et al., 2016</paper>

- For SiGeC layers with similar C content, oxidation anneals will reduce the substitutional-C spectroscopic signature (e.g., ~610 cm−1 FTIR line discussed in processing paper) more strongly than inert anneals at comparable temperatures, and will increase signatures consistent with clustering/redistribution.
- As-grown RTCVD SiGeC compositions within x≈9–16%, y≤1.8% will remain free of detectable SiC (FTIR ~800 cm−1) unless subjected to additional thermal budget or defect injection.
- In MBE-like kinetically limited growth, a temperature window exists where substitutional incorporation is high and clustering is minimal; exceeding it increases bond breakage/roughening and raises the likelihood of non-substitutional carbon configurations.

- At fixed C content, there exists a critical combination of (temperature, time, interstitial injection rate) beyond which SiC nucleation becomes rapid; mapping this would yield a time–temperature–defect-injection ‘TTD’ diagram for SiC precipitation in SiGe:C.
- Carbon nearest-neighbor preference (Si vs Ge) could shift the dominant precipitation pathway: if C strongly avoids Ge, Ge-rich matrices might exhibit faster Ge-depletion shells and earlier SiC nucleation at lower global C than Si-rich matrices.

- If controlled anneals in oxidizing vs inert ambients produce identical Cs retention/clustering behavior, the oxidation-driven interstitial flux mechanism is incorrect or irrelevant for these structures.
- If SiC precipitates form readily in as-grown RTCVD films within the stated growth window despite the reported FTIR null result, then either detection limits dominate or the non-precipitation claim is not robust across reactors/conditions.

- No provided dataset contains quantitative formation energies comparing substitutional C vs SiC precipitate in Si0.8Ge0.2 (the mission’s H6 asks for this but evidence here does not provide numbers).  <paper entityId="paper-f253d7c4609a7c200caeda07a88dc222ba55cad2" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="137240377" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Hall et al., 2004</paper> <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper> <paper entityId="paper-ed370b81064857475585dade7616970e8d40c981" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="14320628" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Stephenson et al., 2016</paper>

s2Metadata.title: Si and SiGe Nanowire for Micro-Thermoelectric Generator: A Review of the Current State of the Art
s2Metadata.abstract: In our environment, the large availability of wasted heat has motivated the search for methods to harvest heat. As a reliable way to supply energy, SiGe has been used for thermoelectric generators (TEGs) in space missions for decades. Recently, micro-thermoelectric generators (μTEG) have been shown to be a promising way to supply energy for the Internet of Things (IoT) by using daily waste heat. Combining the predominant CMOS compatibility with high electric conductivity and low thermal conductivity performance, Si nanowire and SiGe nanowire have been a candidate for μTEG. This review gives a comprehensive introduction of the Si, SiGe nanowires, and their possibility for μTEG. The basic thermoelectric principles, materials, structures, fabrication, measurements, and applications are discussed in depth.

content.title: Metastable Cs retention requires kinetically limited growth and low interstitial injection

content.text: Low-temperature epitaxy can lock carbon onto lattice sites, but oxidation and implantation steps can shake it loose into interstitials/clusters that can seed precipitation.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Process paper: achieving and retaining substitutional C requires controlled low-temperature epitaxial growth (MBE/CVD) with 2D growth conditions and careful thermal-budget management; oxidation and implant damage increase interstitial fluxes and can cause C loss or clustering; oxidation generates higher carbon loss rates than vacuum/inert anneals.  <paper entityId="paper-f253d7c4609a7c200caeda07a88dc222ba55cad2" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="137240377" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Hall et al., 2004</paper>

- Ge:C MBE study: incorporation is kinetically limited; effective incorporation appears above ~450 °C, while above ~475 °C surface roughening and Ge–C bond breakage indicates kinetic/chemical destabilization; multiple probes show no detectable C–C clusters at dilute concentrations when using a Ge4C-core precursor.  <paper entityId="paper-ed370b81064857475585dade7616970e8d40c981" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="14320628" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Stephenson et al., 2016</paper>

content.title: Precursor-imposed local coordination suppresses C–C clustering at dilute levels

content.text: If the precursor keeps carbon bonded to host atoms, carbon atoms are less likely to find each other and cluster, so they stay substitutional at low concentrations.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Ge:C study: Ge4C-core precursor designed such that C is fully surrounded by Ge; authors report no detectable C–C clusters by HRTEM/Raman/NRA-RBS/STEM-EDX and infer substitutional/sp3-like incorporation; a direct bandgap reduction consistent with dilute substitutional C is observed.  <paper entityId="paper-ed370b81064857475585dade7616970e8d40c981" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="14320628" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Stephenson et al., 2016</paper>

- Background mentions E4C-core precursor strategies previously applied to Si1−xCy and SiGeC to encourage substitutional carbon and reduce graphitic clustering (contextual prior art).  <paper entityId="paper-ed370b81064857475585dade7616970e8d40c981" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="14320628" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.1">Stephenson et al., 2016</paper>

- If SiGe:C is grown with an E4C-core precursor under a temperature window that preserves surface host–C bonds, Raman/FTIR signatures of substitutional C will dominate with minimal evidence of C–C clustering at comparable dilute y.
- Increasing oxidation time/temperature at fixed initial Cs in SiGe:C will increase SIMS–HRXRD (or SIMS–FTIR) discrepancies by converting Cs into non-substitutional carbon that is invisible to Cs-specific strain/vibrational markers.

- There exists a sharp crossover in post-growth annealing where interstitial injection flips the dominant sink for C from point-defect complexes to SiC nuclei, producing a time–temperature–interstitial-flux ‘precipitation map’ even at the same total C content.
- In Si1−xGex with high Ge fractions, a sufficiently strong preference of C for Si neighbors could produce spontaneous nanoscale Si enrichment around C-rich regions even before SiC nucleation, creating a measurable Ge-depleted shell signature by APT.

- Grow two SiGe:C sets at identical y and x: one with an E4C-core-like precursor and one with a conventional carbon precursor. If both show equal levels of C–C clustering (TEM/Raman) under identical conditions, the precursor-imposed coordination mechanism is weakened.
- If oxidation/implant anneals do not measurably change the Cs fraction (as inferred by Cs-sensitive probes) relative to inert anneals at the same thermal budget, the interstitial-injection-driven Cs→Ci/Cn conversion hypothesis is weakened.

- No quantitative formation energies, diffusion coefficients, or nucleation barriers are provided in the evidence set, so this theory cannot yet parameterize rates or energetic thresholds for SiC precipitation in SiGe.  <paper entityId="paper-f253d7c4609a7c200caeda07a88dc222ba55cad2" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="137240377" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Hall et al., 2004</paper> <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.0">Li et al., 2021</paper> <paper entityId="paper-ed370b81064857475585dade7616970e8d40c981" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="14320628" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Stephenson et al., 2016</paper> <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper>

s2Metadata.title: Innovative Developpement of Silicon Germanium Alloy Enhanced with Nanoprecipitates by Additive Manufacturing
s2Metadata.abstract: Thermoelectric (TE) devices is presented as an environmentally-friendly technology useful for several niche applications in electricity generation and cooling systems. Recent advances in additive manufacturing (AM) techniques, such as Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), allow manufacturing of a wide range of materials, including TE materials. AM of TE materials open new possibilities in TE devices’ shapes that can facilitate their integration and improve their performance. This work presents the development of silicon germanium (SiGe) alloys by L-PBF process. The first attempt at producing this material resulted in a dense material with promising Seebeck coefficient and thermal conductivity, but its other properties were hindered by mechanical cracking occurring during L-PBF processing. To address this issue, a new approach was studied: nanoprecipitates formation during cooling. Nanoprecipitates can simultaneously enhance TE properties by scattering phonons, and enhance mechanical properties by acting as nucleating agents for silicon germanium matrix, and reduce grain size. It is the first time that such approach is studied in AM of TE materials. A specific study has been performed to define the best nanoprecipitates candidates. Three systems of nanoprecipitates were retained: SiC, WSi2 and MoSi2. This work will present how these nanoprecipitates were chosen, then their impacts on SiGe structural and TE properties.

content.title: Nanoinclusion κ reduction is interface-dominant and sensitive to chemistry, not bracketed by single-contrast continuum bounds

content.text: At nanometer sizes, what matters is the real interface, so simple density- or stiffness-only bounds can miss the MD outcome.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Additive-manufacturing study proposes nanoprecipitates (including SiC) to scatter phonons and lower lattice thermal conductivity, implying a mechanism beyond point-defect scattering and emphasizing precipitate/interface effects.  <paper entityId="paper-ae5f20f78dabfd94851c4851eb2cac2596054626" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="273902266" artifactId="extraction-result-3#uuid-e3.0">Baudry et al., 2024</paper>

- SiC nanowire literature summarized shows strong size/boundary scattering effects leading to large κ reductions at nanoscale dimensions, indicating interfaces/boundaries dominate thermal transport at few-nm scales.  <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.1">Li et al., 2021</paper>

content.title: Si-rich shell tradeoff law: reduced alloy disorder vs increased inclusion/interface scattering

content.text: A Si-rich shell can either help heat flow (less alloy disorder) or hurt it (more interface scattering); which happens depends on shell thickness and particle size.
**Supporting evidence:**

- No direct shell data are provided in the evidence set; however, the general premise that nanoprecipitates scatter phonons (e3.0) and that boundaries at nanoscale dominate κ (e6.1) supports the competing-mechanisms framing for core–shell regions.  <paper entityId="paper-ae5f20f78dabfd94851c4851eb2cac2596054626" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="273902266" artifactId="extraction-result-3#uuid-e3.0">Baudry et al., 2024</paper> <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.1">Li et al., 2021</paper>

- For fixed SiC radius R in SiGe, introducing a thin Si-rich shell will change κ non-monotonically with shell thickness t: small t may increase κ slightly (disorder reduction dominates) but larger t will decrease κ (effective inclusion/interface scattering dominates).
- Atomistic simulations that explicitly include interfacial mixing/roughness will show κ reductions larger than smooth-interface continuum predictions at R ~ few nm.

- A carefully tuned graded shell (continuous SiGe composition gradient) could maximize phonon backscattering over a broader spectrum than a sharp shell, producing κ reductions exceeding both sharp-shell and no-shell cases at the same total Ge content.
- If SiC inclusions induce local ordering (reduced short-range disorder) in surrounding SiGe, κ could rise locally enough that inclusion-containing material has higher κ than homogeneous alloy at certain x and temperature ranges.

- If MD with explicit interfaces consistently falls strictly within density-only and stiffness-only continuum bounds for R ~2 nm across multiple interface chemistries, the interface-dominant/out-of-bracket claim is undermined.
- If adding a Si-rich shell always increases κ regardless of t and R (or always decreases), the proposed competition/tradeoff mechanism is incomplete.

- No direct measurements or simulations of κ for SiGe with embedded SiC precipitates/shells are provided in the evidence set; this theory is mechanistic and awaits quantitative validation.  <paper entityId="paper-ae5f20f78dabfd94851c4851eb2cac2596054626" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="273902266" artifactId="extraction-result-3#uuid-e3.0">Baudry et al., 2024</paper> <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.1">Li et al., 2021</paper> <paper entityId="paper-f253d7c4609a7c200caeda07a88dc222ba55cad2" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="137240377" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Hall et al., 2004</paper> <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper>

paper-ed370b81064857475585dade7616970e8d.displayLabel: Gas Source Techniques for Molecular Beam Epitaxy of Highly Mismatched Ge Alloys

s2Metadata.title: Gas Source Techniques for Molecular Beam Epitaxy of Highly Mismatched Ge Alloys
s2Metadata.abstract: Ge and its alloys are attractive candidates for a laser compatible with silicon integrated circuits. Dilute germanium carbide (Ge1−xCx) offers a particularly interesting prospect. By using a precursor gas with a Ge4C core, C can be preferentially incorporated in substitutional sites, suppressing interstitial and C cluster defects. We present a method of reproducible and upscalable gas synthesis of tetrakis(germyl)methane, or (H3Ge)4C, followed by the design of a hybrid gas/solid-source molecular beam epitaxy system and subsequent growth of defect-free Ge1−xCx by molecular beam epitaxy (MBE). Secondary ion mass spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy and contactless electroreflectance confirm the presence of carbon with very high crystal quality resulting in a decrease in the direct bandgap energy. This technique has broad applicability to growth of highly mismatched alloys by MBE.
