content.title: Metastable substitutional-carbon regime with 3nn ordering before precipitates

content.text: Under suitable growth conditions, carbon mostly sits on lattice sites and forms some ordered C–C pairs, without forming SiC precipitates.
**Supporting evidence:**

- RTCVD Si1-x-yGexCy films (x≈9–16%, y≈0–1.8%) show a ~605 cm^-1 Si–C local vibrational mode attributed exclusively to substitutional carbon; integrated IR intensity and Raman ratios scale linearly with substitutional C content and are essentially independent of Ge content up to 16%.  <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper>

- A Raman satellite near ~630 cm^-1 increases with carbon content and is attributed to 3nn substitutional C–C pairs; satellite/local intensity ratio increases linearly with y up to 1.8%, consistent with short-range ordering rather than precipitation.  <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper>

- FTIR inspection in the 750–800 cm^-1 region finds no SiC stretching-mode absorption (~800 cm^-1) in any measured RTCVD samples; authors explicitly conclude absence of SiC precipitate phase under these growth conditions.  <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper>

- Ge1-xCx grown by MBE using a Ge4C-core precursor shows no detectable C–C clusters by TEM/HRTEM/Raman/NRA-RBS/STEM-EDX at dilute concentrations, consistent with kinetically stabilized substitutional/sp3-like incorporation when chemistry prevents exposed carbon on the growth surface.  <paper entityId="paper-ed370b81064857475585dade7616970e8d40c981" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="14320628" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Stephenson et al., 2016</paper>

- Process-focused discussion emphasizes substitutional carbon is achievable under far-from-equilibrium growth and can be a small fraction of total C; also stresses that Cs is metastable and can be lost/redistributed under later thermal processing.  <paper entityId="paper-f253d7c4609a7c200caeda07a88dc222ba55cad2" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="137240377" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Hall et al., 2004</paper>

content.title: Thermal-budget-activated transition from substitutional C to mobile C and clustering/precipitation tendency

content.text: After growth, thermal processing—especially steps that create lots of defects—tends to push carbon out of substitutional sites and toward clustering/precipitation.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Process discussion distinguishes total carbon (SIMS) from substitutional carbon (HRXRD/Raman/FTIR) and notes discrepancies arise and must be interpreted as differing Cs/Ci ratios; HRTEM is suggested if XRD and SIMS diverge after annealing (indicative of redistribution/clustering).  <paper entityId="paper-f253d7c4609a7c200caeda07a88dc222ba55cad2" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="137240377" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Hall et al., 2004</paper>

- Process discussion states oxidation produces higher carbon loss rates than vacuum/inert anneals; carbon retention depends strongly on Si-cap thickness and overall thermal budget, implying strong processing sensitivity of carbon stability.  <paper entityId="paper-f253d7c4609a7c200caeda07a88dc222ba55cad2" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="137240377" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Hall et al., 2004</paper>

- Process discussion states clustering and redistribution can occur during post-growth thermal processing, with interstitial carbon (Ci) as a consequence of clustering/redistribution during processing.  <paper entityId="paper-f253d7c4609a7c200caeda07a88dc222ba55cad2" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="137240377" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Hall et al., 2004</paper>

- RTCVD as-grown films at 550 °C show substitutional C with no SiC precipitates, providing a baseline that thermal processing (not present there) is a plausible differentiator for precipitation outcomes.  <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_009" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper>

- For Si1-x-yGexCy films in the RTCVD-like substitutional regime, modest changes in Ge fraction within x≈0.09–0.16 will not significantly change the proportionality between IR Si–C integrated intensity and substitutional C, but will change Si–Si Raman shift slopes with y (as observed), allowing decoupled calibration of y and strain.
- Introducing a post-growth oxidation step (vs inert anneal at similar temperature/time) will produce a larger increase in SIMS-total-C vs substitutional-C-proxy disparity and stronger emergence of nonsubstitutional signatures (e.g., additional FTIR/Raman features) than an inert anneal alone.

- If local Si chemical potential can be engineered (e.g., by creating Si-rich nanoscale regions in SiGe), carbon will concentrate there even without forming SiC, enabling designed 'C segregation templates' detectable by APT.
- At sufficiently high y but still below gross precipitation, the 3nn-pair satellite/local intensity ratio will deviate from linearity due to higher-order C ordering motifs; this would provide a spectroscopic route to infer the onset of medium-range order before precipitates appear.

- If in as-grown RTCVD samples with y up to ~1.8% a reproducible ~800 cm^-1 SiC band appears without post-anneal, the 'substitutional/3nn regime before precipitates' statement is false or too broad.
- If oxidation steps do not increase the SIMS vs substitutional-proxy disparity relative to inert anneals at the same thermal budget, then defect-rich processing is not the primary lever controlling carbon redistribution.

- No direct evidence in the provided dataset quantifies energetic preference of C for Si vs Ge nearest neighbors in mixed SiGe, nor does it provide formation energies for SiC precipitation in SiGe; thus the theory cannot assign numeric neighbor-preference energies or precipitation driving forces.  <paper entityId="paper-f253d7c4609a7c200caeda07a88dc222ba55cad2" annotationId="ann_010" corpusId="137240377" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Hall et al., 2004</paper> <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_011" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper> <paper entityId="paper-ed370b81064857475585dade7616970e8d40c981" annotationId="ann_012" corpusId="14320628" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Stephenson et al., 2016</paper>

s2Metadata.title: Si and SiGe Nanowire for Micro-Thermoelectric Generator: A Review of the Current State of the Art
s2Metadata.abstract: In our environment, the large availability of wasted heat has motivated the search for methods to harvest heat. As a reliable way to supply energy, SiGe has been used for thermoelectric generators (TEGs) in space missions for decades. Recently, micro-thermoelectric generators (μTEG) have been shown to be a promising way to supply energy for the Internet of Things (IoT) by using daily waste heat. Combining the predominant CMOS compatibility with high electric conductivity and low thermal conductivity performance, Si nanowire and SiGe nanowire have been a candidate for μTEG. This review gives a comprehensive introduction of the Si, SiGe nanowires, and their possibility for μTEG. The basic thermoelectric principles, materials, structures, fabrication, measurements, and applications are discussed in depth.

paper-ae5f20f78dabfd94851c4851eb2cac2596.displayLabel: Innovative Developpement of Silicon Germanium Alloy Enhanced with Nanoprecipitates by Additive Manufacturing

s2Metadata.title: Innovative Developpement of Silicon Germanium Alloy Enhanced with Nanoprecipitates by Additive Manufacturing
s2Metadata.abstract: Thermoelectric (TE) devices is presented as an environmentally-friendly technology useful for several niche applications in electricity generation and cooling systems. Recent advances in additive manufacturing (AM) techniques, such as Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), allow manufacturing of a wide range of materials, including TE materials. AM of TE materials open new possibilities in TE devices’ shapes that can facilitate their integration and improve their performance. This work presents the development of silicon germanium (SiGe) alloys by L-PBF process. The first attempt at producing this material resulted in a dense material with promising Seebeck coefficient and thermal conductivity, but its other properties were hindered by mechanical cracking occurring during L-PBF processing. To address this issue, a new approach was studied: nanoprecipitates formation during cooling. Nanoprecipitates can simultaneously enhance TE properties by scattering phonons, and enhance mechanical properties by acting as nucleating agents for silicon germanium matrix, and reduce grain size. It is the first time that such approach is studied in AM of TE materials. A specific study has been performed to define the best nanoprecipitates candidates. Three systems of nanoprecipitates were retained: SiC, WSi2 and MoSi2. This work will present how these nanoprecipitates were chosen, then their impacts on SiGe structural and TE properties.

content.title: Inclusion scattering strength rises sharply when inclusion size approaches dominant phonon MFPs

content.text: A few-nanometer SiC particle is big enough to strongly scatter heat-carrying phonons, so κ can drop a lot and depends on particle size.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Mission context states that for two 3C-SiC spheres of radius R embedded in Si0.8Ge0.2 at 300 K, a continuum scattering model brackets κ reduction at R=2.0 nm between 40% (density-contrast-only) and 75% (stiffness-contrast-only) relative to the same alloy without the particle (with surrounding composition held equal).

- Review of SiC nanowires reports strong size dependence of κ and large reductions at nanoscale (e.g., MD/NEMD predicting very low κ for ~4 nm diameter SiC NWs), consistent with strong boundary/interface scattering when dimensions are nanometric.  <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.1">Li et al., 2021</paper>

content.title: Si-rich/Ge-depleted shells reduce alloy-disorder scattering but add gradient/interface scattering

content.text: A Si-rich shell can make the material locally more ‘Si-like’ (less alloy scattering) but also adds extra boundaries; either effect can win.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Mission context specifies that in control runs carbon prefers Si neighbours, so each particle is placed inside a Si-rich (Ge-free) shell about 7 Å thick, implying a chemically reconstructed region around SiC inclusions is physically plausible/considered in simulations.

- RTCVD SiGeC spectroscopy shows substitutional C causes pronounced local bond distortions (phonon frequency shifts), indicating that compositional/chemical perturbations at the atomic scale can significantly modify phonon properties; by extension, a reconstructed shell around an inclusion is expected to influence phonon scattering/velocities.  <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper>

- AM study proposes nanoprecipitates (including SiC) to scatter phonons and improve TE properties, aligning with the idea that inclusions and their surrounding microstructure (grain size/nucleation agents) influence κ, though without quantification.  <paper entityId="paper-ae5f20f78dabfd94851c4851eb2cac2596054626" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="273902266" artifactId="extraction-result-3#uuid-e3.0">Baudry et al., 2024</paper>

- At fixed SiC radius, making the surrounding shell more Si-rich (reducing Ge content) will reduce alloy-disorder scattering in the shell and can partially offset inclusion scattering for short-MFP phonons, producing a smaller κ reduction than a bare inclusion if interfaces are relatively smooth/coherent.
- If the shell is made compositionally graded rather than abrupt, κ will decrease relative to an abrupt coherent shell at the same average composition because gradient scattering broadens phonon reflection across frequencies.

- There exists an optimal shell thickness (order several Å to ~1 nm) that maximizes κ reduction by simultaneously maintaining strong inclusion scattering while avoiding too much 'matrix purification'; beyond this thickness κ reduction weakens.
- Engineered Ge-enriched shells (opposite of Si-rich) could further reduce κ by increasing alloy disorder near the interface, but may be thermodynamically/kinetically difficult; if achievable, it would outperform Si-rich shells for κ suppression.

- If adding a Ge-free Si-rich shell around SiC inclusions always increases κ relative to a precipitate-free SiGe alloy (rather than sometimes decreasing), then the added-interface/gradient scattering channel is overestimated.
- If κ reduction is nearly insensitive to inclusion radius in the 1–5 nm range at 300 K, then the assumed MFP-scale matching is wrong for the simulated/experimental conditions.

- The provided evidence does not include direct measurements/simulations of κ for SiGe with SiC inclusions or with Si-rich shells; thus the theory cannot be numerically calibrated within this dataset.  <paper entityId="paper-ae5f20f78dabfd94851c4851eb2cac2596054626" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="273902266" artifactId="extraction-result-3#uuid-e3.0">Baudry et al., 2024</paper> <paper entityId="paper-f253d7c4609a7c200caeda07a88dc222ba55cad2" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="137240377" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Hall et al., 2004</paper> <paper entityId="paper-68fdda5fd9f5dd1215f91f9d889657944a608187" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="31806986" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Wasyluk et al., 2010</paper> <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.1">Li et al., 2021</paper>
